identity.title: Every Language Model Has a Forgery-Resistant Signature

problem.claim: The work addresses identifying which closed-weight language model produced an output and verifying model outputs through forensic signals.

contributions.claim: Introduces an ellipse-based signature derived from the geometric constraint that language-model outputs lie on a high-dimensional ellipse.
Characterizes the signature as difficult to forge, naturally occurring, self-contained, and redundantly detectable across logprob outputs.
Proposes an output-verification protocol analogous to cryptographic symmetric-key message authentication.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish the ellipse signature from existing output-association methods such as language-model watermarks through its stated geometric basis and properties.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report evaluating a novel ellipse-extraction technique on small models.
The authors report that practical hurdles make ellipse extraction infeasible for production-size models, supporting their characterization of the signature as hard to forge.

narrative_sequence.summary: Closed-weight models with public APIs motivate forensic methods for extracting hidden details and identifying models from outputs.
The paper focuses on geometric constraints imposed by model architecture and parameters, highlighting an underused constraint.
The ellipse signature is presented as distinct from watermarks and as hard to forge, naturally occurring, self-contained, and redundantly detectable.
The authors evaluate ellipse extraction on small models, discuss production-scale hurdles, and propose an output-verification protocol.

source_observation.claim: The abstract makes the signature’s value concrete by listing distinct operational properties—forge resistance, natural occurrence, self-contained detection, and redundancy—before describing evaluation and a verification protocol.

lessons.interpretation: A technical contribution becomes easier to assess when its properties are tied to an explicit adversarial or deployment use case.
lessons.application: When presenting a forensic mechanism, enumerate the threat-relevant properties separately, then connect each to a reported test or downstream protocol.
lessons.exception: This framing is less suitable when the contribution is exploratory and its intended threat model or deployment setting is not yet defined.

unknowns: The abstract does not report quantitative identification, extraction, or forgery rates, nor the exact conditions of the small-model evaluation.
It does not specify the verification protocol’s operational steps, threat model, or production-scale feasibility beyond the stated hurdles.
